1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:9.

2.note: Yahweh is speaking of **Judah** and **her gates** as if they were living things that could mourn and grow weak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah mourn, and those who gather at her city gates grow weak]

Here, **her gates** represents the people who gathered at the gates of her cities for business and legal matters. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the people at her city gates]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Judah, not to the gates mentioned in the previous line. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Judah mourn for the land]

Here, **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the cry of the people of Jerusalem goes up]

3.note: The expression **they are ashamed and confounded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they feel ashamed and dismayed]

The terms **ashamed** and **confounded** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they are utterly humiliated]

Covering the head was a symbolic action by which people of this culture showed that they were ashamed and grieving. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. This also occurs in verse 4. Alternate translation: [and they cover their head to show their shame]

4.q: בַּ⁠עֲב֤וּר הָ⁠אֲדָמָה֙ חַ֔תָּה כִּ֛י לֹא הָיָ֥ה גֶ֖שֶׁם בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ בֹּ֥שׁוּ אִכָּרִ֖ים חָפ֥וּ רֹאשָֽׁ⁠ם
4.note: The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is the reason for the result that comes later in the verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [The farmers are ashamed; they cover their head because the ground is dismayed since there is not rain in the land]

Yahweh is speaking of **the ground** as if it were a living thing that could be **dismayed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ground is parched and cracked]

5.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific **doe**. He means does in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any doe in the field]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [gives birth to her fawn and abandons it]

6.note: The term **bare heights** describes hilltops and ridges on which no trees or plants are growing. If your readers would not be familiar with what bare heights are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [treeless hilltops]

The point of this comparison is that just as **jackals** pant with open mouths, so the wild donkeys are struggling for breath. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they pant with open mouths, struggling to breathe]
See how you translated this phrase in 9:11.

Here, **Their eyes fail** represents the loss of strength and hope that comes from searching for something and not finding it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They grow weak from searching in vain]

7.note: This is the beginning of what Jeremiah said on behalf of the people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Jeremiah. Alternate translation: [And Jeremiah responded,]

Jeremiah is speaking of **our iniquities** as if they were living things that could **testify** in court. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are clearly guilty because of our sins]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things we have done]

Here, **your name** represents Yahweh’s reputation among the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 21. Alternate translation: [for the sake of your reputation]

8.note: Here, **Hope of Israel** represents the one in whom Israel hopes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You in whom Israel hopes]
The pronoun **him** refers to Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one saving Israel]

8.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה תִֽהְיֶה֙ כְּ⁠גֵ֣ר בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וּ⁠כְ⁠אֹרֵ֖חַ נָטָ֥ה לָ⁠לֽוּן
8.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to complain that Yahweh seems to have no interest in the trouble of his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not be like a stranger in the land, and like one traveling who turns aside to lodge!]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a stranger in the land** and **one traveling who turns aside to lodge** have no lasting concern for a place, so Yahweh seems to have no concern for the people among whom he lives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [unconcerned about this land, like someone who has no lasting ties to it]

9.q: כְּ⁠אִ֣ישׁ נִדְהָ֔ם כְּ⁠גִבּ֖וֹר לֹא יוּכַ֣ל לְ⁠הוֹשִׁ֑יעַ
9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a man being confused** and **a mighty one who is not able to save** are powerless to help, so Yahweh seems unwilling to rescue his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [powerless to help us, unwilling to rescue us]

The expression **being confused** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a man who cannot understand what is happening]

The expression **your name is called over us** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you have called us by your name]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:8.

Jeremiah is using **your name is called over us** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we belong to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we belong to you]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not abandon us]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **leave**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [stay with us]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5. This also occurs in verse 15.

In this verse, the word **people** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Judeans as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “people.” Alternate translation: [to these people]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the unfaithfulness of the people were a love to **wander** from place to place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have loved to be unfaithful]

Yahweh is using **their feet** to represent the people themselves and the way they live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have not kept themselves from straying]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Therefore, I do not accept them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **iniquity** and **sins**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [how wickedly they have behaved and will punish them for how they have sinned]

Yahweh is using **he will remember their iniquity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will call them to account for their iniquity.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will call them to account for their iniquity] or [he will hold them accountable for their iniquity]

12.note: This could mean: (1) the pronoun **them** refers to the people who bring the offerings. Alternate translation: [I will not accept the people who offer them] or (2) the pronoun **them** refers to the offerings themselves. Alternate translation: [I will not accept those offerings]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by warfare and by the starvation and by the illness]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would **consume** the people the way a fire burns up what it touches. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy them]

13.note: See how you translated this phrase in 1:6.

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus Yahweh’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

13.q: הַ⁠נְּבִאִ֜ים אֹמְרִ֤ים לָ⁠הֶם֙ לֹֽא תִרְא֣וּ חֶ֔רֶב וְ⁠רָעָ֖ב לֹֽא יִהְיֶ֣ה לָ⁠כֶ֑ם כִּֽי שְׁל֤וֹם אֱמֶת֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָ⁠כֶ֔ם בַּ⁠מָּק֖וֹם הַ⁠זֶּֽה
13.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the prophets are telling them that they will not see sword and they will not have famine, but that you will give them peace of stability in this place]

The prophets are using **see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “experience.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You shall not experience sword]

The prophets are using the possessive form to describe a **peace** that is characterized by **stability**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [stable peace]

14.note: Here, **my name** represents Yahweh’s own authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [claiming my authority]
The word **you** is plural here because it refers to the people of Judah and not to Jeremiah alone, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **vision** that is characterized by **a lie**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a false vision]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **divination**, **worthlessness**, and **deceitfulness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and things they divined and things that are worthless and deceitful things that they have thought up in their hearts]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the thoughts that the prophets make up for themselves were **their heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the deceitful thoughts that they make up themselves]

15.q: כֹּֽה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה עַֽל הַ⁠נְּבִאִ֞ים הַ⁠נִּבְּאִ֣ים בִּ⁠שְׁמִ⁠י֮
15.note: Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh** before speaking of himself in the first person as **my name**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [thus I, Yahweh, say concerning the prophets, the ones prophesying in my name]

15.q: וְ⁠הֵ֨מָּה֙ אֹֽמְרִ֔ים חֶ֣רֶב וְ⁠רָעָ֔ב לֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֖ה בָּ⁠אָ֣רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֑את
15.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and they are saying that there shall not be sword and famine in this land]

16.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the prophets, while the pronoun **them** refers to the people to whom the prophets are prophesying. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to whom those prophets are prophesying, those people shall be]

The expression **being cast out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will throw them out]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the punishment that the people deserve were a liquid that he could **pour out** on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will bring upon them the punishment they deserve]

Here, **their evil** represents the punishment that their evil deeds deserve. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the punishment their wickedness deserves]

17.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֤ אֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ אֶת הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תֵּרַ֨דְנָה עֵינַ֥⁠י דִּמְעָ֛ה
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell them to let your eyes flow with tears]

Jeremiah is referring to all of the time by naming two major components, **night** and **day**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [continually]
The pronoun **them** refers to Jeremiah’s **eyes**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and let my tears not stop flowing]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **cease**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and let them continue]

Jeremiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The expression **she has been broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [an enemy has broken her]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Judah were a **virgin daughter** who had been severely wounded. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my dear and helpless people]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:6.

18.q: אִם־יָצָ֣אתִי הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֗ה וְ⁠הִנֵּה֙ חַלְלֵי־חֶ֔רֶב וְ⁠אִם֙ בָּ֣אתִי הָ⁠עִ֔יר וְ⁠הִנֵּ֖ה & תַּחֲלוּאֵ֣י רָעָ֑ב
18.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [If I go out to the field, then behold, I see those who have been pierced by the sword, and if I enter the city, then behold, I see those who are dead from famine]

18.q: אִם יָצָ֣אתִי הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֗ה & וְ⁠אִם֙ בָּ֣אתִי הָ⁠עִ֔יר
18.note: Jeremiah is referring to every place in the land by naming two major components, **the field** and **the city**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [If I go anywhere throughout the land … and if I look all around]

Jeremiah is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what Jeremiah is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [I go out to the field]

Jeremiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [then there before me are]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **pierced ones** who are characterized by **the sword** and **diseases** that are characterized by **famine**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [ones pierced by the sword … the diseases caused by famine]

Here, **pierced ones of the sword** represents people who have been killed in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [those killed in battle]

Jeremiah is not referring to a specific **prophet** or a specific **priest**. He means prophets and priests in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [both prophets and priests]

19.q: הֲ⁠מָאֹ֨ס מָאַ֜סְתָּ אֶת יְהוּדָ֗ה אִם בְּ⁠צִיּוֹן֙ גָּעֲלָ֣ה נַפְשֶׁ֔⁠ךָ
19.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to express his distress at what Yahweh has allowed to happen to his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have utterly rejected Judah! You truly loathe Zion!]

This is the beginning of what Jeremiah said to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Jeremiah. Alternate translation: [Jeremiah asked Yahweh, “Have, rejecting]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **rejected** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Have you totally rejected]

Jeremiah is using **your soul** to represent Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have you loathed]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the disaster that has come upon the nation were a wound for which there is **no healing**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why have you harmed us so that we cannot recover]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **healing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that no one can heal us]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and we hoped for a time of healing]

19.q: קַוֵּ֤ה לְ⁠שָׁלוֹם֙ וְ⁠אֵ֣ין ט֔וֹב וּ⁠לְ⁠עֵ֥ת מַרְפֵּ֖א וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה בְעָתָֽה
19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:15.

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means “**and** we hoped **for a time of healing, but behold, terror**.” You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and we hoped for a time of healing, but look, instead there was only terror]

20.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wickedness** and **iniquity**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [that we have acted wickedly, and that our fathers acted sinfully]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the ancestors of the people were their **fathers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the iniquity of our ancestors]

21.note: Here, **the throne of your glory** represents Yahweh’s rule over his people from the place where he dwells among them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your glorious reign over us]
The people are using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. Alternate translation: [For the sake of who you are, do not spurn us]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **spurn**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [please favor us]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **disgrace**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [honor the throne of your glory]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Remember us]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please remember us. Please do not break your covenant with us]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **break**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [keep your covenant with us]

22.q: הֲ⁠יֵ֨שׁ בְּ⁠הַבְלֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ מַגְשִׁמִ֔ים וְ⁠אִם הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֖יִם יִתְּנ֣וּ רְבִבִ֑ים
22.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that neither **the idols of the nations** nor **the heavens** are able to produce rain. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There are none among the idols of the nations who can bring rain, and the heavens cannot give showers!]

Jeremiah is using the question form to affirm that Yahweh alone is the one who sends rain. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You are indeed the one, Yahweh our God!]

The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why we will wait]
